planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown crowns in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade sheltered from wind; growth is slow the first year but fills in vigorously by the second and third seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, protected from drying wind that can shred the brittle stipes. 'Encourage' is a selection out of the old Victorian 'Vernoniae Cristatum' group of lady fern, distinguished by pinnae that are tasseled or crested along their full length rather than just at the frond tip, giving the whole light-green frond a dense, frilly texture. It was one of the top-rated taxa in the Chicago Botanic Garden's decade-plus comparative Athyrium trial, forming a robust, vase-shaped clump by its second year and holding up well through Midwestern winters. Keep soil consistently moist during hot spells, since some afternoon sun can scorch the fine-textured foliage if the ground is allowed to dry out.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Soul Mate Dwarf Japanese Painted Fern

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; because of its small stature, site it where competing foliage won't crowd it out and keep soil from drying between waterings.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, siting it toward the front of a bed where its diminutive scale won't be lost among larger neighbors. 'Soul Mate' is the smallest named Japanese painted fern cultivar in general circulation, forming a tight spreading mound under a foot tall and wide with the same silvery-green, purple-flushed coloring as the species but in miniature proportions. Because it is more sensitive to sun exposure than larger-growing painted fern cultivars, it performs best with reliable afternoon shade and even soil moisture; plants sited in too much sun tend toward desiccated, tattered fronds by midsummer. Its small size makes it well suited to trough gardens, shaded rock gardens, and the front edge of a woodland border where full-size painted ferns would overwhelm the scene.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this selection tolerates a bit more afternoon sun than typical lady ferns provided soil moisture is kept consistent.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. 'Dre's Dagger' is a sport of the Victorian-era lady fern cultivar 'Victoriae', sharing its parent's distinctive crisscrossed, X-patterned pinnae along the rachis and nodding, fan-shaped frond tips, but on narrower fronds held in a strongly vase-shaped, upright habit. Despite its reputation as a dwarf form, it grows nearly as large as 'Victoriae' itself in good garden soil. It builds into a dense clump within two to three seasons and has shown good tolerance of hot afternoon sun without significant leaf scorch when soil moisture is adequate, making it a reliable choice for a crested-fern accent among hostas, heucheras, or other shade perennials.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in consistently moist, rich soil in partial to full shade; this western native wants more water than the Eurasian type variety and thrives along streambanks or in boggy woodland soil.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, along stream banks, pond margins, or in low woodland spots that stay damp through summer. Western lady fern is the Pacific Coast and Rocky Mountain native variety of common lady fern, ranging from Alaska south into California and east to the Rockies, where it grows naturally in seepage areas and wet forest understories and can reach considerably larger proportions than the eastern type variety. Its bright green, finely divided, tapering fronds arch outward from a stout upright crown in a classic shuttlecock form, producing new growth steadily through the season. It is an excellent large-scale choice for naturalizing a consistently moist shade garden or rain garden where a bold textural fern is wanted.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; give it reliable shade from afternoon sun, as this older selection is more prone to leaf scorch than many modern lady fern cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, keeping it out of hot afternoon sun. 'Vernoniae Cristatum' is one of the original Victorian-era lady fern selections, dating to late-nineteenth-century England, and is distinct from the plainer 'Vernoniae' form in that each plant produces a mix of tasseled, crested fronds alongside ordinary unadorned ones, giving a looser, less uniformly lacy look than fully crested modern cultivars. It is typically among the earliest lady ferns to emerge in spring, forming a broadly vase-shaped clump of bright green foliage. Because its foliage can desiccate in hot, dry conditions, site it in consistently moist, well-shaded ground for the best long-term appearance.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade for best winter survival; this feathery form is less reliably winter hardy than ordinary lady fern cultivars, so avoid planting in exposed sites.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade, where it is best protected from both hot sun and harsh winter exposure. 'Plumosum Axminster' belongs to the historic English Plumosum group of lady fern, prized since Victorian times for finely dissected, plumose fronds that give the whole plant a softer, lacier texture than the species; its broad, lime-green leaves form a consistently good vase-shaped clump through the growing season. It is more cold-sensitive at the crown than many other lady fern selections, so a reliably shaded, sheltered planting site and a protective winter mulch in colder zones will help it persist over multiple seasons. Use it as a textural specimen where its delicate, feathery foliage can be appreciated up close.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in sharply drained soil in part sun to light shade; its thick, compact leaves tolerate more sun and drought than typical holly fern once roots are established.

directions: Plant in sharply drained soil in part sun to light shade; established plants handle dry shade and brief drought far better than standard holly fern. 'Eco-Korean Jade' (also offered as 'Eco Korean Lace') is a naturally dwarf coastal form of Japanese holly fern collected by plantsman Barry Yinger on Baengnyeongdo Island off the Korean coast and first distributed by the late Don Jacobs; its thick, glossy, dark green leaflets and dense, compact habit are adaptations to the battering salt winds of its wind-scoured cliff-top origin. Topping out around six to eight inches tall and roughly fifteen inches wide, it is considerably hardier in cold than typical Cyrtomium falcatum, a trait inherited from its northerly Korean provenance. Its small scale and toughness make it a natural for rock gardens, trough plantings, and the front edge of a shaded border.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; growth is slow to establish compared to the vigorously running species, so be patient the first couple of seasons.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, in low spots, pond margins, or boggy woodland ground where the species itself would naturally spread. 'Dwarf Form' is a rarely offered, slow-growing miniature selection of common sensitive fern, reaching only a few inches tall and wide compared to the knee-high, aggressively running species, which makes it far better behaved in small garden settings. Like the species, its sterile fronds have broad, wavy-margined pinnae and the plant colors attractively in autumn before going dormant; unlike the species, it spreads gradually rather than running wide through the bed. Its diminutive scale suits it to shaded container plantings, trough gardens, or the margin of a small water feature where the full-size species would quickly overwhelm its neighbors.
